# Software Architecture and Microservice Workshop

*Building effective software efficiently*

## Starting point

This is the forth part of the Software Architecture and Microservices workshop.
It builds upon the previous section.

## From Monolith to Distributed

Our current monolithic application has been partitioned by domain and refactored
into separate projects and repositories. While each team can work on its
application segment independently, all changes are integrated into a single
stream to produce a fat JAR file, ensuring the application functions as
expected.

The monolithic architecture style has several limitations:

1. **Deploying the whole application**: Even minor changes to one part of the
   system require redeploying the entire application. Such extensive
   redeployments can introduce new bugs, increasing the risk with each update.
2. **Single process**: The entire application runs as a single process. If any
   component fails—for example, through a memory leak—it impacts the entire
   application. To mitigate this, teams often reduce deployment frequency and
   slow the introduction of new features.

An alternative is a distributed architecture, where each component operates as
an independent service, commonly known as microservices. However, it is
important to recognise that not all distributed systems qualify as
microservices. Simply having several Spring Boot projects does not constitute a
microservices architecture.

> **What is the difference between Service-Oriented Architecture and microservices?**
>
> Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) and microservices both build systems from
> services, but they differ in scope and design philosophy. SOA was created to
> integrate heterogeneous enterprise systems (such as ERP, CRM, and legacy
> applications) through coarse-grained services, often mediated by a central
> Enterprise Service Bus (ESB) that handles routing, orchestration, and
> transformation. Services in SOA may share databases, rely on extensive
> governance, and use standards such as SOAP and WSDL, with the primary goal of
> interoperability and reuse across the enterprise.
>
> Microservices, by contrast, focus on decomposing a single application into
> small, fine-grained services that are independently deployable, loosely
> coupled, and aligned to business domains. Each microservice owns its own data
> store, communicates via lightweight protocols such as REST or messaging, and
> avoids centralised integration layers in favour of decentralised, autonomous
> teams. Whereas SOA is about enterprise-wide integration, microservices are
> about agility, scalability, and the rapid evolution of an application.
>
> The following diagram illustrates the difference between these two approaches.
>
> ![Difference between a service oriented architecture and microservices](./assets/images/SOA%20and%20Microservices.png)

> **Should we simply adopt microservices?**
>
> Distributed systems, while offering significant benefits, also introduce
> complexity. By dividing a monolithic application into a distributed system, we
> trade some advantages for others. For example, microservices can address the
> limitations of redeploying a monolithic application as a single process, but
> they also require sophisticated coordination and can complicate development.
>
> In our case, transitioning to a distributed architecture may not be advisable.
> Given our application’s scale and the current effectiveness of a single team,
> microservices could complicate rather than simplify our operations.
> Microservices are often most beneficial for managing large-scale applications
> with multiple teams, where team size itself becomes the bottleneck. Industry
> best practice suggests keeping teams smaller than 15 people; beyond this,
> efficiency tends to decline. In such contexts, splitting responsibilities into
> microservices can address both technical scalability and team management
> challenges.

> **What do you mean by “*team size is the actual bottleneck*”?**
>
> Have you ever tried to organise a dinner with a small group of friends?
> Finding a date when everyone is available and a restaurant that everyone likes
> can be more difficult than it seems.
>
> Similarly, managing a large team can become the bottleneck of a project.
> Achieving consensus and agreeing on a way forward in a large group can take
> longer than the actual work required. That is what I mean by
> “*team size is the actual bottleneck*”: the slowest component in the process
> is the team’s size itself.
>
> According to
> [Dunbar’s number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunbar%27s_number), a team
> should ideally not exceed 15 individuals, reflecting the limit of close social
> relationships one person can maintain.
>
> Conversely,
> [Google’s Project Aristotle](https://www.thinkwithgoogle.com/intl/en-emea/future-of-marketing/management-and-culture/five-dynamics-effective-team/)
> found no correlation between team size and effectiveness.
>
> From my experience, larger teams tend to be less effective than smaller ones.
> Reaching agreement takes longer, subgroups or cliques form, and rivalry often
> emerges, which is rarely productive. While I have not conducted quantitative
> research, I have consistently found smaller teams to be more effective.
>
> For example, suppose you want to introduce mutation testing to improve test
> quality. In a smaller team, this might affect five other developers; in a
> larger team, it could affect twenty. Convincing five developers is challenging
> enough—now imagine having to persuade twenty.

In our monolithic architecture, all requests are managed through a single entry
point. As we transition to a split architecture with two independent
services—one for the cart and one for the catalogue—we introduce two separate
entry points. Consequently, callers must know the specific service endpoint they
wish to access, complicating interactions.

![Two separate points of entry](./assets/images/Two%20separate%20points%20of%20entry.png)

For instance, if the cart component needs to fetch data from the catalogue, it
must know the catalogue’s current location. This complicates service management,
as any change in a service’s location requires updating the endpoints known to
all consumers. Such changes demand that both the old and new endpoints remain
available during the transition, increasing rollback complexity and potentially
causing prolonged use of a faulty service by slower-to-update consumers.

A practical solution is to implement a reverse HTTP/S proxy. A reverse proxy is
a web server that receives HTTP/S requests and forwards them to the appropriate
service. While it does not handle the request logic itself, it often adds
headers to requests. This approach routes all traffic through a single proxy
server, which then directs requests to the correct backend service. The main
advantage is that consumers interact through a unified endpoint, simplifying
their experience and reducing the need to track individual service locations.

![Reverse Proxy](./assets/images/Reverse%20Proxy.png)

When service endpoints change—whether due to updates, relocations, or scaling
operations—only the reverse proxy configuration requires adjustment. Consumers
remain unaffected, as the proxy abstracts the backend details. Additionally,
service providers can often manage these changes through self-service portals
that validate and apply updates automatically.

The role and implementation of reverse proxies will be discussed further in the
following section, covering deployment, security, and maintenance considerations
to ensure optimal operation and minimal disruption to consumer services.

![Monolithic Architecture Style - Single Database](./assets/images/Monolithic%20Architecture%20Style%20-%20Single%20Database.png)

Once we separate the cart and the catalogue, this approach will no longer be possible.

![Distributed (Microservices) Architecture Style - Multiple Databases.png](./assets/images/Distributed%20Microservices%20Architecture%20Style%20-%20Multiple%20Databases.png)

> **Can we simply share one database?**
>
> Yes, technically this is possible, and it is referred to as the
> **service-based architecture style**. This is sometimes used as an
> intermediate step when migrating from a monolithic to a microservices
> architecture.
>
> However, I would not recommend this approach, not even as a starting point.
> Splitting a database is difficult, and in some cases nearly impossible. If we
> cannot separate the database, should we continue with a shared one? A shared
> database is widely considered an
> [anti-pattern](https://microservices.io/patterns/data/shared-database.html),
> as the database effectively becomes part of the API. Changing it requires
> coordination between all teams using it, which demands their collective
> agreement. For instance, if *Team A* needs a change but *Team B* does not have
> the capacity to adapt, progress stalls.
>
> In one consultancy engagement, I worked with a team maintaining a large
> monolithic Java application with a shared database and shared data model.
> Their time to market was severely constrained: changes often took weeks to
> reach production. After analysis, we discovered that the shared model and
> database—not the size of the codebase—were the true bottlenecks.
>
> To return to the question: while technically feasible, I strongly advise
> against this approach. It creates a false sense of progress during refactoring
> but slows down future change. It represents technical debt with very high
> interest and should only ever be incurred when no alternatives exist.

> **Can we share the catalogue database?**
>
> Yes, this approach follows the
> [reporting database design pattern](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/ReportingDatabase.html).
> Rather than sharing a single database, a dedicated, read-only reporting
> database can be shared with other components. In our example, the catalogue
> creates a new table, such as `reporting_catalogue_item`, which the cart
> component uses to fetch the information it requires. The cart can only read
> from this table, and the catalogue is restricted from modifying the table
> structure, or at a minimum, must maintain backwards compatibility.
>
> Please note that reporting tables are considered part of the API.
> Consequently, they must maintain backwards compatibility and support
> versioning. Reporting tables can be versioned by appending a version number,
> for example, `reporting_catalogue_item_v1`. When changes are required to the
> source table, a new reporting table is created with the updated structure,
> while the original version is retained.

> **What is the difference between a component and a service in software architecture?**
>
> A **component** is a unit of software design and organisation within an
> application. It encapsulates a set of responsibilities, hides its internal
> details, and exposes well-defined interfaces to the rest of the system. For
> example, in a monolithic e-commerce application, the cart and catalogue can
> each be implemented as components: the cart component manages shopping carts,
> while the catalogue component manages product information. Both live inside
> the same deployable application and interact through in-process calls.
>
> A **service**, by contrast, is a runtime construct: an independently
> deployable and executable part of the application that exposes its
> functionality via a network interface, such as a REST API. Using the same
> example, if the cart and catalogue are deployed as separate processes, each
> with its own API and possibly its own database, they are considered services.
> Together, these services form a distributed application. In short, components
> are about *code organisation and modularity*, while services are about
> *deployment and runtime interaction*.

When exchanging data between components such as the cart and the catalogue,
there are two communication patterns: synchronous and asynchronous. In a
**synchronous communication pattern**, the caller sends a request and waits for
a response before continuing—for example, a REST API call where the client is
blocked until the server replies. In an **asynchronous communication pattern**,
the caller sends a message without waiting for an immediate response, allowing
both sides to proceed independently—common in message queues, event streams, or
publish–subscribe systems.

The cart depends on data owned by the catalogue to function. This data can be
retrieved synchronously by having the cart request it from the catalogue via
REST. The catalogue already provides such an endpoint, and the cart can use this
to obtain the required information. I must stress, however, that this approach
is strongly discouraged, for reasons that will be explained later.

### Reverse Proxy

A reverse HTTP/S proxy is a type of server that sits in front of web servers and
forwards clients’, such as web browsers, requests to those web servers. It acts
as an intermediary for requests from clients seeking resources from servers that
provide those resources.

The reverse proxy receives requests from clients and forwards them to the
appropriate server. After the server handles the request, the reverse proxy
relays the response back to the client. This process is transparent to the user,
who interacts with the proxy as if it were the server itself.

By distributing client requests across multiple servers, a reverse proxy
effectively balances the load, ensuring no single server becomes overwhelmed.
This improves the responsiveness and reliability of the service.

Reverse proxies can cache outgoing responses from a server. When a new request
comes in for the same resource, the proxy can provide the cached response,
significantly reducing the load on the server and speeding up response times.

A reverse proxy can provide an additional layer of defense by shielding backend
servers from direct internet exposure. This setup helps to mitigate security
threats.

It makes it easier to scale web applications by adding, removing, or replacing
servers without disrupting the client experience. Configuration changes are made
on the proxy, which simplifies backend service management.

Centralising TLS termination at the reverse proxy (handling HTTPS connections)
offloads this task from the backend servers, simplifying TLS management and
improving performance.

Reverse proxies are widely used in various configurations for enhancing
performance, security, and reliability of websites and web services. Examples
include popular web servers like [Nginx](https://www.nginx.com/) and
[Apache](https://httpd.apache.org/), which are often configured as reverse
proxies.

According to
[Google Trends](https://trends.google.com/trends/explore?date=today%201-m&q=%2Fm%2F02qft91,Httpd,%2Fm%2F0r4vbb0&hl=en-GB),
Nginx is the most popular amongst Apache and
[HAProxy](https://www.haproxy.com/). Therefore, we will be using Nginx as our
reverse HTTPS proxy. In this example we do not make use of TLS, and thus we will
not configure TLS termination.

We will start by creating a directory where we will put all configuration
related to our reverse proxy. The configuration will be versioned controlled
like other source code so that we can keep track of changes. This is referred to
as
[infrastructure as code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infrastructure_as_code),
where all configuration is version controlled and in some cases its deployment
is too automated through as CI/CD pipeline. Unfortunately, we will not take it
as far in this workshop.

All requests to our application are handled by either the cart controller or the
catalogue controller. The reverse proxy can be already configured to redirect
traffic to `/cart` to the cart and `/catalogue` to the catalogue, as shown in
the following table.

| Path        | Endpoint                         |
| ----------- | -------------------------------- |
| `/cart`     | `http://ADDRESS:PORT/cart`       |
| `/catalogue`| `http://ADDRESS:PORT/catalogue`  |

For this demo, we will run the reverse proxy as a container while the services
will be running on the host machine, accessible through `host.docker.internal`.

| Path         | Endpoint                                     |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| `/cart`      | `http://host.docker.internal:8082/cart`      |
| `/catalogue` | `http://host.docker.internal:8081/catalogue` |

> **Why can we not simply pass all requests to the application?**
>
> Our application is currently a monolithic application running as a single
> process—assuming we are not scaling the application horizontally. This means
> that all requests are handled by this single process. Once the application is
> split into multiple processes—for example, one for the catalogue and another
> for the cart—we will have two separate processes, and therefore, two points of
> entry.
>
> We can introduce a third process to act as the application’s entry point,
> similar to what we have when running as a monolith. This third process would
> act as a router, redirecting traffic to the appropriate component.
>
> This approach offers more than just a single point of entry. When refactoring
> larger applications, we can progressively carve out functionality and redirect
> traffic to new components without impacting users.
>
> Given the size of this application, I have decided to split all traffic from
> the outset. However, this is not the only available approach; as mentioned
> before, we can add new redirections incrementally.
>
> In our case, this is the simplest solution. Once the catalogue and cart
> projects are extracted into standalone services (microservices), we can simply
> update their respective paths.

We will be running this as a container in our local host. Create the
`Dockerfile` that pulls the
[current latest version (`1.31.8`) of Nginx](https://hub.docker.com/_/nginx/tags)
and copies the configuration.

> **Why not use the `latest` tag?**
>
> The `latest` tag is very convenient as we don’t have to keep track of the
> current latest version. But it also breaks the reproducibility concept. By
> using the specific version, we ensure that this version of Nginx is used no
> matter when this container image is built. When we decide to move to a newer
> version, we do this intentionally by changing the version number in the code.
>
> When we build (or compile) our code, or a container image, we only expect
> things to change when we actually change the code. Compiling the same class
> twice should produce the same output. The same principle should apply to
> container images. When using the `latest` tag, we may obtain a different
> container just because the `latest` tag now points to a new version.
>
> Say that a newer version of Nginx is incompatible with our existing
> configuration. Using the `latest` tag, we will pull the current latest version
> which is incompatible with our configuration, and thus it will not work as
> expected. Our application will not work as expected despite the fact that we
> didn’t change the code.
>
> Do not use or rely on the `latest` tag as this breaks reproducibility.

> **Do container repositories guarantee reproducibility?**
>
> Any tag can be overwritten, therefore no.
>
> Say we create a container image and we tag it with version `1.23`. We can make
> some changes to our container image and tag the new version with `1.23`, thus
> overwriting the previous version.
>
> Needless to say that this is a dangerous practice and one should do so
> cautiously. Public images, such as Nginx, should avoid such practices as these
> break reproducibility.
>
> Container engines, such as [Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/), are able to
> revert to a previous container if the new one does not work. They provide a
> convenient fallback mechanism. Say we change our service and tag this with
> `latest`. Kubernetes will notice a change in the container repository and pull
> the latest version. All works fine until we introduce a bug that prevents the
> new version of the application to start.
>
> When the new container image fails to start, Kubernetes will try to fall back
> by pulling the previous version. Given that we use the same tag for all
> versions, that is `latest`, Kubernetes pulls the currently broken container
> image and tries again. As you imagine, it will enter an endless loop and our
> application will fail to start compromising availability.
>
> While it may be harmless locally, overwriting a tag of a container image that
> is published and shared with others breaks reproducibility.

### Observability

In 2015, [Honest Update](https://x.com/honest_update) posted a now well-known
tweet:

> “*We replaced our monolith with microservices so that every outage could be more like a murder mystery.*”
> ([reference](https://x.com/honest_update/status/651897353889259520?lang=en))

Amusing as it is, there is a great deal of truth in this. Distributed systems
introduce significant accidental complexity, which makes debugging issues more
challenging. Two services may function perfectly well in isolation but still
exhibit unexpected behaviour when combined. Problems may arise from network
unreliability (dropped packets), latency due to service proximity or traffic
levels, serialisation overhead (reduced throughput), and more. These issues do
not typically affect a monolithic architecture, where—aside from database or
third-party service calls—all method invocations are intra-process.

With a monolith, we have a single application to debug. Logs and metrics are
collected in one place, making it straightforward to trace a request through the
system. Once the application is split into multiple services, this simplicity is
lost. Each service produces its own log stream, and correlating them becomes
necessary. The ability to trace a single request across the whole system is no
longer available out of the box. For example, debugging the cart service ends as
soon as it calls the catalogue service to retrieve item details.

Fortunately, we are not alone in facing this challenge. Various solutions exist,
one of the most effective being **distributed tracing**. In this approach, each
request is tagged with a unique identifier that is carried throughout its
lifecycle. When the cart calls the catalogue, it passes the trace id with the
request, enabling us to follow the request end-to-end across the application
rather than being confined to a single service.

Spring Boot integrates seamlessly with [Micrometer](https://micrometer.io/), a
vendor-neutral observability framework for the JVM. Micrometer allows us to
collect metrics and traces from our application and send them to a backend of
choice. Switching between backends requires minimal change to the application.
Another widely used framework is [OpenTelemetry](https://opentelemetry.io/),
which, unlike Micrometer, is language-agnostic and supports many ecosystems
beyond Java. According to
[Google Trends](https://trends.google.com/trends/explore?cat=32&q=OpenTelemetry,Micrometer&hl=en-GB),
OpenTelemetry is searched more often, likely reflecting its broader
applicability across programming languages. In this example, we will use
OpenTelemetry, which also integrates well with Spring Boot.

Setting up OpenTelemetry can be a little involved, so we will focus on
distributed tracing to demonstrate its value. Ideally, observability should also
include centralised logging and metrics, but adding those would require
additional time and effort.

> **Is OpenTelemetry all or nothing? Do we need to implement this across the entire application for it to be effective?**
>
> No. OpenTelemetry (or any observability tool such as Micrometer) does not have
> to be applied everywhere at once. For example, we could start by instrumenting
> only the catalogue service, and later extend this to the cart service. While
> partial adoption will not give us a complete picture, it still provides
> valuable insights into the instrumented services. In practice, it is advisable
> to start small—apply observability to one or two services, evaluate the
> impact, and then decide whether to roll it out further.

> **Are there overheads associated with observability tools and frameworks?**
>
> Yes—there is no such thing as a free lunch.
>
> Even basic logging has a measurable impact on application performance. For
> instance, compare the runtime of a simple loop with logging at every iteration
> against the same loop without logging; the difference is noticeable.
> Nevertheless, logs and telemetry data are essential—and in some cases required
> for compliance.
>
> Java provides
> [JDK Flight Recorder (JFR)](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/java-components/jdk-mission-control/9/user-guide/using-jdk-flight-recorder.html),
> a very low-overhead mechanism for collecting key runtime information. Instead
> of traditional logs, we can emit
> [JFR events](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/jfapi/create-events.html),
> which impose less overhead on the application. These events can then be
> exported as JFR files and inspected using
> [JDK Mission Control](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/jdk-mission-control.html)
> or similar tools.

### Jaeger

The data collected by OpenTelemetry needs to be sent to an external system so it
can be accessed independently of the application and its services. In a
distributed architecture, with multiple services—and often several instances of
the same service running on different machines—there must be a central location
where all traces are collected and rendered.

To keep this workshop simple, we will focus only on tracing and collect the data
in a [Jaeger](https://www.jaegertracing.io/) instance. Jaeger will serve both as
the central collector and as the visualisation tool. OpenTelemetry can export
trace data directly to Jaeger using its
[Jaeger exporter](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/java/exporters/#jaeger).

### Architecture Decision Records (ADR)

In the previous sections, we discussed three important architectural decisions:
splitting the application into two components (the catalogue and the cart),
using a reverse proxy to act as a single point of entry and route traffic to the
respective component, and introduce OpenTelemetry.

These three decisions are recorded in separate architectural decision records
(ADRs), `ADR-008`, `ADR-009`, `ADR-010`. `ADR-007` has now been superseded by
`ADR-008`, and its status has been updated accordingly.

Lastly, update the `README.md` file, which summarises all ADRs, to clearly
indicate that `ADR-007` has been superseded by `ADR-008`.

### Test the application

Please note that this architectural change does not modify the underlying
business logic. The business logic remains exactly as it was, without any
alterations.

Build and test the application

```shell
./mvnw clean package
```

Create the reverse proxy container

```shell
(
  cd 'reverse-proxy' &&
  docker build \
    --file 'Dockerfile' \
    --tag 'application-distributed-rest-synchronous:reverse-proxy' \
    --load \
    .
)
```

Run the reverse proxy container and wait for it to start. Requests to `/`
return [`404`](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP_404) because the proxy only
routes the `/catalogue` and `/cart` endpoints. Requests to those endpoints
require the corresponding services to be running.

Publish host port `8080` to Nginx's port `80` inside the container using
`--publish 8080:80`. We avoid host port `80` because Linux commonly restricts
ports below `1024` to privileged processes. Rootless container runtimes can
therefore fail to publish port `80` with a permission-denied error. Using
`8080` avoids requiring elevated privileges or changes to the host's security
configuration for this workshop.

Access the application through `http://localhost:8080`, as in the previous
examples. Nginx forwards catalogue requests to port `8081` and cart requests
to port `8082` on the host; each service keeps its own listening port.

```shell
docker run \
  --rm \
  --detach \
  --name 'application-distributed-rest-synchronous-reverse-proxy' \
  --publish 8080:80 \
  --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
  'application-distributed-rest-synchronous:reverse-proxy' || exit 1

# Wait for Nginx to start
# The root path is not routed, so a 404 confirms that Nginx is responding
until [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/')" -eq '404' ]; do sleep 1; done
```

Request the root path to try the reverse proxy. Expect a `404` because `/` is
not routed; this confirms that Nginx is responding before we start the services.

```shell
curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/'
```

Nginx 404 response

```html
<html>
<head><title>404 Not Found</title></head>
<body>
<center><h1>404 Not Found</h1></center>
<hr><center>nginx/1.31.8</center>
</body>
</html>
```

The simplest way to start a Jaeger instance is with Docker, using the
[`jaegertracing/all-in-one:1.74.0` image](https://hub.docker.com/r/jaegertracing/all-in-one/tags).

```shell
docker run \
  --rm \
  --detach \
  --name 'application-distributed-rest-synchronous-jaeger' \
  --env COLLECTOR_ZIPKIN_HOST_PORT=:9411 \
  --publish 4317:4317 \
  --publish 4318:4318 \
  --publish 9411:9411 \
  --publish 16686:16686 \
  'docker.io/jaegertracing/all-in-one:1.74.0'

# Wait for Jaeger to start
until [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:16686/search')" -eq '200' ]; do sleep 1; done
```

You can access the Jaeger user interface at
[http://localhost:16686/search](http://localhost:16686/search). At this stage,
our services will not yet appear, as Jaeger has not received any trace data from
them.

Start the catalogue service before testing the cart service. The cart service
depends on the catalogue service to function; the two exhibit Connascence of
Execution.

> **What is Connascence?**
>
> Connascence is a software design concept that describes the degree of
> interdependence between components. It comes in two broad forms:
>
> - **Static Connascence**: Dependencies that exist at compile time. Examples
>   include requiring another module’s class (Connascence of Type) or relying on
>   a specific method name (Connascence of Name). Static connascence is visible
>   in the code and can usually be detected and resolved through refactoring.
>   Reducing static connascence improves modularity and allows teams to work
>   more independently.
> - **Dynamic Connascence**: Dependencies that exist only at runtime. Examples
>   include one component needing another to be available (Connascence of
>   Execution) or two components depending on data being in a consistent state
>   (Connascence of Value). Dynamic connascence cannot be fully eliminated in
>   distributed systems, but it can be managed through patterns such as retries,
>   eventual consistency, caching, or messaging.

> **Which should we aim for?**
>
> We should strive to **minimise static connascence** to keep codebases loosely
> coupled and maintainable. Dynamic connascence, on the other hand, is often
> unavoidable—especially in distributed systems—but it should be made
> **explicit, deliberate, and well-managed** rather than hidden. In short:
> reduce static connascence where possible, and design carefully for dynamic
> connascence.
>
> In the monolithic design, the cart component depended directly on
> `CatalogueItemEntity` from the catalogue project. This created
> **static connascence of type**: any change to the catalogue entity class could
> break the cart at compile time.
>
> After introducing the `CatalogueItemGateway` and transfer objects, this
> compile-time dependency was removed. The cart and catalogue are now statically
> independent.
>
> At runtime, however, the cart still needs the catalogue component to provide
> item details. This is **dynamic connascence of execution**: the cart cannot
> function fully if the catalogue is unavailable.
>
> Thus, we improved the design by reducing static connascence, while accepting
> and managing the unavoidable dynamic connascence.

```shell
# Start the catalogue application in the background and wait for it to be ready
java -jar './catalogue/target/application-distributed-rest-synchronous-catalogue-1.0.0.jar' > './catalogue/target/application.log' 2>&1 &

# Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
echo "$!" > './catalogue/target/application.pid'

# Wait for the application to start
until [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/1')" -eq '200' ]; do sleep 1; done
```

This starts the catalogue service in the background and waits until it is ready
to handle requests. The catalogue service listens on port `8081` and is
accessible through the reverse proxy at `http://localhost:8080/catalogue`.

Make a few requests to the catalogue items endpoint. We have the following

Add a new item to the catalogue.

We will add a new item named `Green Plant`, with the description:
`Put a little life in your living room!`. The response will then be saved to a
file so that we can use the generated id to retrieve the item later.

```shell
# Save the response in a file as we will use it later on
curl --silent \
  -X POST 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"caption":"Green Plant","description":"Put a little life in your living room!!"}' \
  | jq \
  > new-catalogue-item.json

# Print the output
jq . new-catalogue-item.json

Fetch this item using the generated id.

# Fetch the new item
curl --silent "http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/${ITEM_ID}" | jq
```

The newly added item

  "id": 6,
  "caption": "Green Plant",
  "description": "Put a little life in your living room!!"

Let’s run the cart service together with the catalogue service. Remember, the
cart service depends on the catalogue service and cannot function without it.

```shell
# Start the cart application in the background and wait for it to be ready
CATALOGUE_ROOT_URI='http://localhost:8080/' \
  java -jar './cart/target/application-distributed-rest-synchronous-cart-1.0.0.jar' > './cart/target/application.log' 2>&1 &

# Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
echo "$!" > './cart/target/application.pid'

# Wait for the application to start
until [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/cart/1')" -eq '200' ]; do sleep 1; done
```

This starts the cart service in the background and waits until it is ready
to handle requests. The cart service listens on port `8082` and is accessible
through the reverse proxy at `http://localhost:8080/cart`.

Everything worked as expected. By opening
[http://localhost:16686/](http://localhost:16686/), we can explore the traces
generated by our application.

![Distributed Tracing](./assets/images/Distributed%20Tracing.png)

Our services do not need to be running in order to access Jaeger.

Some organisations have even replaced large architecture diagrams with
distributed tracing tools such as Jaeger or [Zipkin](https://zipkin.io/).
These provide a real-time view of the entire application by capturing
communication both within individual services and between services.

Of course, observability introduces overhead. Each service collects and
transmits data to the central collector (Jaeger in our example), which consumes
CPU, memory, and network resources. In most cases, the benefits outweigh the
costs, but it is important to monitor this and adjust the sampling rate to avoid
overwhelming the infrastructure on which the application runs.

We can now stop both the reverse proxy and the Jaeger instance.

```shell
docker stop 'application-distributed-rest-synchronous-jaeger'
docker stop 'application-distributed-rest-synchronous-reverse-proxy'
```

### Tradeoffs

Splitting a monolith into synchronous services (HTTP/REST) trades in-process
calls for network hops. You gain independent deployability and clearer ownership
boundaries (e.g., cart and catalogue teams ship on their own cadence), but you
pay a latency and reliability tax: every request can now fail due to timeouts,
DNS, TLS, rate limits, or partial outages. Architects must add timeouts, retries
with jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, idempotency, and fallbacks to prevent
cascades (e.g., a slow catalogue service stalling the cart’s “add to basket”).
This also raises the bar for observability—you’ll need tracing across services,
structured logs, and SLOs to diagnose cross-service issues quickly.

You also exchange simple, ACID, in-process transactions for distributed
coordination. Cross-service workflows (cart → payment → fulfilment) require
patterns like sagas, outbox/inbox, and compensating actions instead of 2PC.
Strong consistency becomes harder; you’ll often settle for read-your-write
within a service and eventual consistency across services. This affects user
experience: for example, the cart may briefly show stale catalogue prices unless
you introduce caches, versioned contracts, or “verify at checkout” logic.

Operationally, you move from one build and deploy pipeline to many pipelines.
That improves team autonomy but increases operational complexity and cost:
service discovery, API gateways, TLS, schema/API versioning, dependency
upgrades, and capacity management per service. Testing shifts from mostly
unit/integration to include contract tests and end-to-end journeys across
services; release coordination becomes a matter of backwards-compatible APIs and
phased rollouts. Security posture changes too: a larger attack surface requires
service-to-service auth (mTLS/JWT), least privilege, and stricter network
policies.

Finally, consider organisation and cognition. Micro-boundaries aligned to
domains reduce within-team cognitive load but raise system-wide cognitive load:
developers must understand failure modes over the network, retries, and partial
availability. Without clear domain boundaries, product-team ownership, and
platform tooling, a distributed system can underperform a well-structured
modular monolith. In short: you gain speed of independent change and resilience
isolation if—and only if—you invest in resilience patterns, observability,
compatible contracts, and platform automation**.

With cart and catalogue split into services communicating via REST, deployment
frequency (4/5) improves because services can be deployed independently. For
example, updating the catalogue API doesn’t require redeploying the cart.
However, the need for API versioning slows lead time (3/5), as dependent
consumers (like the cart) must be updated carefully.

The change failure rate (3/5) is moderate. Failures in one service (e.g.
catalogue returning errors) can cascade to others (cart cannot show items),
unless resilience patterns (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers) are
implemented. Similarly, MTTR (3/5) depends on good observability: if catalogue
fails, cart requests may pile up until the issue is diagnosed. Logs and traces
help, but distributed debugging is harder than in a monolith.

From a developer perspective, cognitive load (3/5) is higher: engineers must
understand service APIs, infrastructure, and network behaviour. Satisfaction
(3/5) is balanced — teams gain more autonomy but deal with operational
complexity. Communication (3/5) shifts to managing service contracts: the cart
and fulfilment teams must coordinate API expectations, but they don’t need to
edit the same codebase.
